notes: Consistently attributed to Malcolm Forbes across quotation collections, and it matches the aphoristic register of his 'Fact and Comment' column in Forbes magazine and the 'Thoughts on the Business of Life' compilations. I cannot place a specific issue, page, or book from training knowledge, so the attribution rests on secondary consistency rather than a primary source. No competing claimant that I know of.

Marc Allen (New World Library founder, author of 'Visionary Business' and 'The Millionaire Course') is a plausible modern popularizer, but the three-tier fool/smart/wise structure is a long-standing proverbial form with many older analogues, notably the aphorism commonly given to Bismarck ('Fools say they learn by experience; I prefer to profit by others' experience') and the 'learn from the mistakes of others, you can't live long enough to make them all yourself' family attributed variously to Eleanor Roosevelt, Groucho Marx, and Hyman Rickover. I cannot confirm that Allen originated this wording, and I will not guess a true source.

earliest_print_source: La Prisonniere (The Captive), vol. 5 of A la recherche du temps perdu, Marcel Proust, 1923
notes: Genuinely Proust in substance, but this popular English form is a compression, not a translation. The original runs closer to: 'The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others...' ('Le seul veritable voyage... ce ne serait pas d'aller vers de nouveaux paysages, mais d'avoir d'autres yeux'). Source is real and datable; the recorded wording should be understood as a paraphrase.

earliest_print_source: Albertine disparue / The Fugitive (also published as The Sweet Cheat Gone), vol. 6 of A la recherche du temps perdu, Marcel Proust, 1925
notes: Renders Proust's 'On ne guerit d'une souffrance qu'a condition de l'eprouver pleinement,' from the late volumes of the Recherche dealing with the aftermath of Albertine. I am confident of the author and the work; I am less certain of the exact volume boundary, since the passage is sometimes cited from The Fugitive and sometimes from The Captive. Wording is a standard translation rather than a folk paraphrase.

earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book VIII, 47 (c. 170-180 CE)
notes: Meditations VIII.47. George Long's translation reads 'If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now.' The recorded text is that translation modernized in pronouns only; the sense and structure are exact.

earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book II, 5 (c. 170-180 CE)
notes: Condensed from Meditations II.5, commonly rendered 'Perform every act in life as though it were thy last' or 'do everything as if it were the last thing you were doing in your life.' A closely related formulation appears at II.11. Author and work are secure; the recorded line is a shortened translation.

Margaret Gatty (1809-1873), author of 'Parables from Nature' and 'The Book of Sun-Dials' (1872), is the name attached to this line in quotation collections, and the epigrammatic form is consistent with the sundial mottoes she gathered. But I cannot confirm whether she wrote it, translated it, or merely recorded it from an older inscription, and I have no page or edition to cite. Deliberately leaving the print source null rather than guessing at The Book of Sun-Dials.

The well-documented form of this line belongs to John W. Gardner (Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare; founder of Common Cause): 'We are continually faced by great opportunities brilliantly disguised as insoluble problems,' associated with his mid-1960s writing and speeches. The saying has also drifted to Lee Iacocca and Charles Swindoll, and the Margaret Mead version appears in collections without any source in her published anthropological work. I know of no Mead text containing it. Confidence figure reflects the strength of the Mead attribution, which is weak.

Margaret Stortz is a Religious Science / New Thought minister and author, and the sentiment fits that tradition's gratitude-and-attraction idiom, but I have no specific book, article, or sermon in training knowledge that carries this passage. I cannot rule out that it circulates from an anthology or daily-reader compilation. No competing attribution known; the honest answer here is that I cannot place it.

Consistently attributed to Marian Wright Edelman and consistent in voice and content with the numbered life lessons in 'The Measure of Our Success: A Letter to My Children and Yours' (1992), which is where I believe it originates. I am not certain enough of the lesson number or wording in that book to record it as a citation, so the print source stays null. No competing claimant.

earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976 - Text, Ch. 1, 'Principles of Miracles', principle 3
notes: This is not original to Marianne Williamson. It is, essentially verbatim, the third of the Fifty Miracle Principles that open the Text of A Course in Miracles: 'Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.' Williamson's 'A Return to Love' (1992) is a commentary on ACIM and quotes the Course extensively, which is how the line came to be tagged with her name. The attribution to her is a quoter-for-author error.
suggested_reattribution: A Course in Miracles (Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976)

earliest_print_source: A Return to Love: Reflections on the Principles of A Course in Miracles, Marianne Williamson, 1992 (ch. 7)
notes: Correctly attributed here, and worth protecting: this passage is one of the most-misattributed texts in circulation, routinely credited to Nelson Mandela's 1994 inaugural address, which does not contain it. Williamson has confirmed authorship. Two wording notes on the recorded text: the original punctuates 'inadequate.' as a full stop before 'Our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond measure,' and the recorded version omits the sentence 'You are a child of God' that follows 'who are you not to be?' - a common secular truncation.

The voice, vocabulary, and subject matter are strongly consistent with Williamson's writing on romantic love, most plausibly 'Enchanted Love: The Mystical Power of Intimate Relationships' (1999) rather than 'A Return to Love.' The ellipses indicate the text was stitched from a longer passage, which is typical of a real book excerpt but also makes it hard to match. I cannot confirm the book or page from training knowledge, so no citation is recorded.

Widely and consistently attributed to Marianne Williamson, and forgiveness-as-world-healing is a central and repeated theme of her work. I cannot locate a specific book or page. One caution given q_0961 in this same batch: Williamson's writing is saturated with A Course in Miracles material, so there is a residual risk that a line like this restates Course teaching; I do not recognize it as verbatim ACIM, but I flag the possibility rather than certify the attribution above the promotion bar.

I believe this comes from Marie-Louise von Franz's chapter 'The Process of Individuation' in 'Man and His Symbols' (C. G. Jung, ed., 1964), which is her best-known writing in English and matches this passage's theme of renewal through attending to the unconscious. The editorial bracket '[of renewal]' suggests the corpus entry was taken from a careful print quotation rather than a meme. I am not confident enough of the chapter or page to record it as a citation, so the print source stays null and the attribution rests on style and subject match plus consistent secondary citation.

Consistently attributed to Marilyn Ferguson, author of 'The Aquarian Conspiracy' (1980) and editor of the Brain/Mind Bulletin, and the framing of fear as information matches her idiom. The passage's length and structure suggest an excerpt from her writing rather than an aphorism assembled by anthologists. I cannot confirm the book or issue, so no citation is recorded.

One of the most-reproduced lines credited to Marilyn Ferguson, with consistent attribution but, as far as I know, no cited source anywhere in that circulation. Short aphorisms of this kind are the ones most likely to be detached from an author or absorbed from workshop culture, so consistent repetition is weak evidence on its own. Plausibly hers - it reads like a condensation of the same material as q_0966 - but unverified.

Solidly and consistently attributed to Mario Andretti in interviews and racing literature, though I cannot name the original interview or date. Important wording caveat: the canonical form is 'If everything seems under control, you're not going fast enough.' The recorded text ('feels under control ... just not driving fast enough') is a drifted variant. Recommend normalizing to the standard wording before promotion.

Genuine Twain, from the closing chapter of The Innocents Abroad: 'Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry, and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things cannot be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one's lifetime.' The recorded entry is lowercased and truncated mid-sentence; it should be capitalized and either closed with a period or extended to the full clause.

The pre-flag is correct. No such line appears in Twain's published work, letters, or notebooks, and the attributions to him begin decades after his death in 1910 - the earliest instance I know of is a 1970 John Robert Colombo 'found poem' that presents 'History never repeats itself but it rhymes' as a Twain saying, which is a repetition of the claim rather than evidence for it. I cannot identify a true originator, so no reattribution is offered; classifying as apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed for exactly that reason. See also q_0975, a near-duplicate of this entry.

The pre-flag is correct: no source in Twain's published work or correspondence. The same sentence circulates just as often under Ralph Waldo Emerson's name, and that attribution is equally unsourced - Emerson's actual related line, from 'Heroism,' is 'Always do what you are afraid to do,' which he credits to his aunt Mary Moody Emerson. Because both major claimants fail and I cannot identify a real origin, apocryphal with no reattribution.

earliest_print_source: Pudd'nhead Wilson, Mark Twain, 1894 - epigraph to ch. 12, from 'Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar'
notes: Genuine Twain, unlike the three neighbouring entries in this batch. It appears as a Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar epigraph and continues '...except a creature that has no fear, in which case courage would be meaningless.' The original punctuates with a dash: 'Courage is resistance to fear, mastery of fear - not absence of fear.' The recorded comma is a minor deviation.

earliest_print_source: P.S. I Love You, H. Jackson Brown Jr., 1990
notes: The pre-flag matches what I know. Nothing in Twain's corpus contains this, and 'throw off the bowlines / sail away from the safe harbor' is not his register. The earliest documented appearance is in H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s 'P.S. I Love You' (1990), a collection of sayings from his mother, Sarah Frances Brown; the Twain tag attached afterwards and spread through 1990s self-help and graduation-speech material. Recording the true origin here because it is documented, not inferred - but note that Brown's book presents it as his mother's saying, so 'H. Jackson Brown Jr.' is the compiler rather than strictly the author.
suggested_reattribution: Sarah Frances Brown, as recorded by her son H. Jackson Brown Jr. in P.S. I Love You (1990)

notes: Not pre-flagged, but it should have been. No Twain source exists for this. It is a wordy variant of the unsourced 'Worrying is like paying a debt you don't owe,' which circulates under Twain, Will Rogers, and others without a citation for any of them. The one genuinely documented aphorism in this family belongs to William Ralph Inge, Dean of St Paul's: 'Worry is interest paid on trouble before it falls due.' The recorded wording differs enough that I will not reattribute it to Inge, but his line is the likely ancestor of the metaphor. Recommend flagging this entry as suspect.

Same verdict as q_0970, of which this is a near-duplicate differing only by the word 'does' - the corpus is carrying both variants and should deduplicate. No Twain source; attributions post-date his 1910 death by decades, with the earliest I know of being John Robert Colombo's 1970 found poem. No identifiable true author, hence apocryphal with no reattribution.
